fields.title: Journey Map: Where Exactly Things Go Wrong
fields.keyTakeaway: A journey map is only as useful as it is grounded in observation. Drawn from memory by the team, it just freezes your assumptions and makes them look like data.
fields.checkQuestion: There are seven stages on the map and exactly one drop in emotions. What should you check first?
fields.blocks/0/text: The same question about how a person solves the task right now, but **unfolded over time**: not just one moment, but the entire journey.
fields.blocks/1/subtitle: Rows without which a map is just a diagram
fields.blocks/1/items/0: **Stages** — by the user's steps, not by your screens.
fields.blocks/1/items/1: **Actions** — what they do, including what they do outside the product.
fields.blocks/1/items/3: **Touchpoints** — where they interact with you: product, support, email, invoice.
fields.blocks/1/items/4: **Pain points and opportunities** — takeaways for each stage, not a general one.
fields.blocks/2/text: The most valuable part of the map is **steps outside the product**. That is usually where the pain lives, and that is exactly what analytics misses: calling an employee, recalculating in another tool, messaging an accountant.
fields.blocks/3/text:
The map was drawn based on seven interviews. Stages: set schedule → publish → changes during the week → close the month.

At the "changes" stage, they found a step that isn't in the product at all: the owner calls the employee to make sure they saw the shift swap. This takes 10–20 minutes a week and causes the most frustration.

In product analytics, this step is invisible: there is simply no event for it. They found it only because they asked about the entire journey, not just screens.
fields.blocks/3/title: Smena, a step that wasn't in the product
fields.blocks/4/text: A map shows a typical journey and hides variation: for a chain of six locations, it's different, and averaging is more dangerous than having no map at all. Build it by segments. Also, a map gets outdated — six months after changes, it's a museum piece on the wall.
